clinical_category: Rheumatoid arthritis - interpretation of rheumatoid factor testing
blueprint_topic: Interpretation of autoimmune laboratory findings in clinical context
stem: A client has symmetric inflammatory small-joint symptoms suspicious for rheumatoid arthritis. The rheumatoid factor result is negative. Which interpretation by the nurse is most accurate?

options.A: A negative rheumatoid factor does not rule out rheumatoid arthritis; the result must be interpreted with the clinical pattern and other findings such as anti-CCP antibodies, inflammatory markers, and imaging when indicated.
options.B: A negative rheumatoid factor excludes rheumatoid arthritis, so no additional rheumatologic evaluation is appropriate.
options.C: Rheumatoid factor is diagnostic by itself, so only a positive RF can establish rheumatoid arthritis regardless of symptoms.
options.D: Rheumatoid factor has no useful role in rheumatoid arthritis evaluation and should never be considered with other clinical information.

rationale: A is correct. Current NIAMS guidance states that rheumatoid arthritis has no single diagnostic test. Rheumatoid factor is one useful laboratory finding, but not every person with RA tests positive, and some people without RA or with other diseases can have a positive RF. Anti-CCP antibodies, inflammatory markers, the history and physical examination, and imaging may all contribute to evaluation. Therefore, a negative RF does not exclude RA in a client with a compatible inflammatory joint pattern. B and C incorrectly treat RF as an all-or-none diagnostic test. D is incorrect because RF can support the diagnosis when interpreted appropriately. The final item converts the source's abstract sensitivity/specificity statement into a practical interpretation problem without requiring memorization of a numerical test-performance percentage.
educational_objective: Interpret rheumatoid factor as supportive rather than definitive evidence in rheumatoid arthritis and recognize that a negative RF does not exclude the disease when clinical findings remain compatible.
source_organization: National Institute of Arthritis and Musculoskeletal and Skin Diseases (NIAMS), National Institutes of Health
source_document_title: Rheumatoid Arthritis: Diagnosis, Treatment, and Steps to Take
source_locator: NIAMS 'Rheumatoid Arthritis: Diagnosis, Treatment, and Steps to Take' → Diagnosis: there is no single test for RA; Laboratory Tests → Rheumatoid factor: not all people with RA test positive, some people with positive RF never develop RA, and RF can be positive in other diseases; RF is interpreted with other tests and clinical evaluation. Same section → anti-CCP, ESR, CRP and imaging may support diagnosis and disease assessment.
source_claim_supported: Current NIAMS guidance directly supports the limitations of RF testing, the fact that negative RF does not exclude RA, and the need to interpret RF with clinical findings and additional laboratory/imaging information.
blueprint_source_organization: National Council of State Boards of Nursing (NCSBN)
blueprint_locator: Physiological Integrity → Reduction of Risk Potential: monitor and interpret diagnostic and laboratory findings, compare findings with the client's clinical presentation, and recognize when further evaluation is needed.
correction_summary: Rebuilt the source's abstract sensitivity/specificity statement into an applied negative-RF interpretation. The final item uses current NIH/NIAMS guidance, avoids unsupported numerical sensitivity/specificity estimates, and prevents both false exclusion after a negative RF and false diagnostic certainty after a positive RF.
audit_findings: The source's core statement was clinically valid but abstract and relied on a generic ACR page rather than a precise current diagnostic-information locator.
Fresh NIAMS review directly states that RA has no single diagnostic test and that RF can be negative in RA or positive without RA.
The final item tests a clinically consequential negative-RF interpretation rather than memorizing a sensitivity/specificity concept.
Distractors test false exclusion, RF-only diagnosis and dismissal of RF's supportive role; none is defensible.
